You are writing a plain-language summary of an as-filed Tennessee House bill for an adult reader without legal training.

Use only the bill text supplied in the user message. Treat it as a proposal at introduction, not as proof that it became law or describes current law. Do not use outside knowledge, bill descriptions, later legislative history, or the unstated contents of cited statutes.

Write a neutral summary in prose. Start with what the bill would change. Cover its distinct material provisions, including affected people or organizations, new or changed duties and rights, eligibility rules, amounts and thresholds, deadlines, exceptions, reporting or enforcement requirements, and effective dates when stated. Preserve the bill's conditions and legal distinctions; do not turn a permission into a requirement or a proposal into an enacted rule.

Use familiar words and short, complete sentences. Explain a technical term when the supplied text gives enough context; otherwise retain it rather than guess. Distinguish background or WHEREAS statements from operative provisions, and mention background only when it helps explain the bill. If the bill amends or repeals a cited section without showing that section's contents, describe the textual change and citation without inventing the prior rule or its wider effects.

Keep the summary substantially shorter than the source while retaining the main independent changes. A very short bill may need only one or two sentences; a multi-section bill may need several short paragraphs. Do not add opinions, predicted consequences, a readability score, a confidence rating, headings, bullet points, or a list of citations. Return only the fields required by the supplied output schema.

Bill number: HB1772

<bill_text>
HOUSE BILL 1772

 By Raper

 AN ACT to amend Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 9;
 Title 28; Title 29; Title 40 and Title 49, relative to
 offender reentry.

BE IT ENACTED BY THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY OF THE STATE OF TENNESSEE:

 SECTION 1. Tennessee Code Annotated, Title 40, Chapter 29, Part 1, is amended by

adding the following as a new section:

 (a) In any proceeding on a claim against a higher education institution for

 negligence in admitting, enrolling, extending housing opportunities to, or otherwise

 facilitating the educational attainment of a person who has been previously convicted of

 a criminal offense, a higher education institution is not liable based solely upon the fact

 that the person has been previously convicted of a criminal offense.

 (b) In a cause of action against a higher education institution for negligence in

 admitting, enrolling, extending housing opportunities to, or otherwise facilitating the

 educational attainment of a person who has been previously convicted of a criminal

 offense, evidence that the person has been previously convicted of a criminal offense is

 not admissible.

 (c) Subsections (a) and (b) do not apply when:

 (1) The higher education institution had actual knowledge of the person's

 prior conviction for a violent offense, as defined in § 40-35-120(b), or a violent

 sexual offense, as defined in § 40-39-202; or

 (2) The higher education institution, having actual knowledge of the

 person's commission of a violent offense, as defined in § 40-35-120(b), or a

 violent sexual offense, as defined in § 40-39-202, after admittance, was willful in

 allowing the person to continue enrolling in, residing at, or otherwise utilizing the

 higher education institution.

 (d) This section does not create a cause of action or expand an existing cause of

 action.

 (e) Section 1-3-119 relative to implied rights of action applies to this section.

 (f) As used in this section, "higher education institution" includes, but is not

 limited to, a school, college, university, or other type of entity offering educational

 credentials, instruction, or educational services primarily to persons who have completed

 or terminated the person's secondary education or who are beyond the age of

 compulsory high school attendance for the attainment of educational, professional, or

 vocational objectives.

 SECTION 2. This act takes effect July 1, 2026, the public welfare requiring it, and

applies to claims arising on or after that date.
</bill_text>

message.reasoning_content:
*   Bill Number: HB1772.
    *   Purpose: To amend Tennessee Code Annotated relative to offender reentry.
    *   Key Provision (Section 1):
        *   Protects higher education institutions from liability based *solely* on the fact that a person admitted, enrolled, given housing, or facilitated education was previously convicted of a criminal offense.
        *   Makes evidence of a person's prior criminal conviction inadmissible in negligence lawsuits against the institution for these reasons.
        *   Exceptions: The protections do not apply if the institution had actual knowledge of a prior conviction for a "violent offense" (§ 40-35-120(b)) or a "violent sexual offense" (§ 40-39-202), or if the institution willfully allowed a person with such a known violent/sexual offense to continue enrolling, residing, or utilizing the institution.
        *   Clarifications: Does not create or expand a cause of action. Section 1-3-119 (implied rights of action) applies.
        *   Definition: "Higher education institution" includes schools, colleges, universities, or entities offering credentials/instruction/services to those who finished secondary education or are past compulsory school age.
    *   Effective Date (Section 2): July 1, 2026, for claims arising on or after that date.

    *   Target audience: Adult without legal training.
    *   Format: Plain-language summary in prose.
    *   Requirements: Neutral, no outside knowledge, start with changes, cover material provisions, preserve conditions/distinctions, short sentences, explain technical terms if context allows, distinguish background from operative, substantialy shorter than source.
    *   Restrictions: No opinions, no predicted consequences, no readability scores, no confidence ratings, no headings, no bullet points, no list of citations. Return only required fields.

    *   *What it changes:* This bill would limit the liability of higher education institutions when dealing with people who have prior criminal convictions.
    *   *Material provisions:*
        *   A higher education institution cannot be held liable for negligence in admitting, enrolling, housing, or facilitating education for someone just because that person has a prior criminal conviction.
        *   Evidence of a person's prior conviction is not allowed in lawsuits against these institutions regarding these actions.
        *   Exceptions: These protections don't apply if the institution knew the person was convicted of a violent offense or a violent sexual offense. They also don't apply if the institution knew about such an offense and willfully let the person continue to enroll, live there, or use the institution's services.
        *   Scope: "Higher education institution" includes colleges, universities, and other entities providing credentials or services to people who have finished high school or are past the age of compulsory attendance.
        *   Legal note: The bill does not create or expand any right to sue.
    *   *Effective date:* July 1, 2026, for claims arising on or after that date.

    *   *Drafting:* This bill would limit the legal liability of higher education institutions that admit, enroll, house, or provide educational services to people with prior criminal convictions. It would prevent these institutions from being held liable for negligence based solely on a person's criminal history. In such lawsuits, evidence of the person's prior conviction would be inadmissible.

    *   These protections would not apply if the institution had actual knowledge that the person was convicted of a violent offense or a violent sexual offense. The protections also would not apply if the institution knew about such an offense and willfully allowed the person to continue enrolling, residing, or using the institution.

    *   A higher education institution is defined as a school, college, university, or similar entity that offers credentials, instruction, or services to people who have completed secondary education or are past the age of compulsory high school attendance. This bill does not create or expand any right to sue.

    *   The bill would take effect on July 1, 2026, and would apply to claims arising on or after that date.

    *   Deadlines/effective dates? Yes.
    *   Preserved legal distinctions? Yes.
    *   Familiar words/short sentences? Yes.
    *   No outside knowledge? Yes.
